name: story
title: Story
description: The vertical format: a sequence of frames a player moves through, with the game's own state laid over the top. It is a `media-frame` and a `hud` plus a pager, two step controls, a caption plate, a way out and one thing to do from here. It owns no more of the media than the frame does: it never plays, never advances on its own and never counts elapsed time. The host owns `step` and the story tells it which way the player asked to go, so an out-of-range step is clamped rather than thrown and a story with no frames still renders the frame's empty state at full size rather than collapsing. Every control carries a name and the pager is a readout rather than a row of extra tab stops, with each cell naming itself complete, current or to go, so the position is readable without colour and without shape. The pager is a deliberate placeholder for the shared segmented track, GSUI-115's `segments` with `presentation="pager"`; folding it in is GSUI-126.
docs: Pass `frames`, one entry per frame, each with a `label` saying what belongs in it, an optional `detail` for the caption plate and an optional `media` node, which is yours and is rendered untouched. Pass `step`, 1-based, and `onStep`, which is called with the step the player asked for: the story renders the step you give it and never moves on its own, so advancing, auto-advancing and deciding a frame is finished are all yours. Pass `hud` and the game state lays over the media as a `hud`, which owns every number in it; read the score through `[data-gs-component="hud"] [data-gs-stat="score"]` rather than the first `[data-gs-value]` on the page. Pass `onSkip` for a way out, which renders no Skip control at all when you omit it, and `action` for the one thing to do from here. `busy` and `playing` are per frame and go straight through to the media frame, which never infers either. Nothing in this library makes the media play. Creating the element, starting it, advancing it and reporting where it got to are your application's job. Pass `gestures` to work it the way a phone's stories work: tap the right of the frame for the next frame and the left third for the one before, swipe across to do the same, and swipe down to put it away. The story follows the finger, shrinks a little and rounds its corners, then closes through `onSkip` past a third of its height or on a fast flick, and springs back otherwise. `onHold` says a finger is down so you can pause your own timer, and `onDismissProgress` says how far it has gone so you can fade what is behind it. It is off by default, so a host with gestures of its own is not answered twice.
